column4: In this chapter we will study the authority and power of Christ, which authorities and powers He has delegated to us (His church), and how to operate in the authority of the name of Jesus. We will also study angelic and demonic beings and examine their authority, power, and natures.
column5: In this chapter we will learn about the authority and power of Christ, the authorities and powers He has delegated to us (His church), and how to operate in the authority of the name of Jesus. We will also learn about angelic and demonic beings, and we will look at their authority, their power, and their characteristics.

column4: Authority means having the right to act. Power is the ability to carry it out. Both are essential in the spiritual life. Authority is different from power. Let’s look at the following table which compares authority & power and consider a few examples.

column4: Here are a few examples to help understand the difference between power and authority.
column5: Here are a few examples to understand the difference between power and authority.

column4: Example 1: At work, an employee may have the talents and skills to conduct a sale of the company's assets (power). This power is lawful if they also have the associated permission (authority) from the company’s owners. Without this authority, selling the company's assets is theft.
column5: Example 1: At work, an employee may have the talent and skills to carry out the sale of the company's assets (power). column4: Example 2: A police officer is given special training in weapons and hand-to-hand combat to learn how to apprehend and physically compel a criminal (power). Police officers have been given the job responsibility backed up by laws (authority) to enforce criminal statutes.

column4: ## The Source of Jesus’ Authority
column5: ## The Source of Jesus' Power

column4: Now that we have looked at precisely what authority is we need to know who the source of that authority is. Jesus’ authority is both divine and delegated. It originates from God the Father, is affirmed through His death and resurrection, and operates in perfect harmony with the Father’s will. Though absolute, His authority respects human free will, demonstrating God’s love rather than forceful control.
column5: Now that we have properly examined what power is, we need to know who the source of that power is. Jesus’ power is divine and delegated. It comes from God the Father, is confirmed by His death and resurrection, and operates perfectly in accordance with the will of the Father. Although it is absolute, His power respects human free will, revealing God’s love rather than a rule by force.

column4: Jesus’ authority is rooted in His divine identity as the Son of God and is granted by the Father. The Father entrusted all authority to Christ, including judgment and rule over heaven and earth (Matthew 11:27). Jesus’ authority reflects the unity and love within the Trinity, where the Son carries out the Father’s plan perfectly (John 3:35).
column5: Jesus’ power is rooted in His divine identity as the Son of God, and it is given by the Father. The Father has entrusted Christ with all authority, including the rule and dominion of heaven and earth (Matthew 11:27). Jesus’ power reflects the unity and love within the Trinity, wherein the Son perfectly carries out the Father’s plan (John 3:35).

column4: While Jesus had inherent authority as God’s Son, His victory over sin, death, and hell was fully established through His death and resurrection. Christ’s obedience in His sacrifice led to His exaltation (seated at the right hand of the Father), securing His authority over all creation. By conquering death, Christ gained absolute dominion over life and eternity.
column5: Although Jesus possessed inherent power as the Son of God, His victory over sin, death, and hell was fully accomplished and confirmed through His death and resurrection. Christ’s obedience in His sacrifice led to His exaltation (seated at the right hand of the Father), securing His authority over all creation. By overcoming death, Christ obtained absolute dominion over life and eternity.

column4: ## Laying on of Hands
column5: ## Laying On of Hands

column4: The laying on of hands is a significant biblical practice used throughout both the Old Testament and New Testament to symbolize blessing, commissioning, healing, and the impartation of spiritual authority or gifts. It is more than just a physical act-it represents a spiritual connection and transfer under the direction of God’s authority.
column5: The laying on of hands is an important biblical practice used in both the Old and New Testaments to signify blessing, appointment/sending, healing, and the impartation of power or spiritual gifts. It is more than a mere physical act—it represents a spiritual connection and transmission under the authority of God.

column4: In the Old Testament, the laying on of hands was often associated with blessing and dedication. For example, Jacob blessed his grandchildren, Ephraim, and Manasseh, by laying his hands on them (Genesis 48:14). Similarly, Moses laid hands on Joshua to commission him as his successor, imparting leadership authority and wisdom (Numbers 27:18-23, Deuteronomy 34:9). This act publicly signified God’s selection and empowerment for the task ahead.
column5: In the Old Testament, the laying on of hands was often associated with blessing and consecration/dedication. For example, Jacob blessed his grandchildren, Ephraim and Manasseh, by laying his hands on them (Genesis 48:14). Likewise, Moses laid his hands on Joshua to appoint his successor, imparting leadership authority and wisdom (Numbers 27:18-23, Deuteronomy 34:9). That act clearly demonstrated God’s choice and empowerment for the task ahead.

column4: In the New Testament, the laying on of hands is closely tied to the ministry of Jesus and the early church. Jesus regularly laid hands on the sick to heal them (Mark 6:5, Luke 4:40), demonstrating both compassion and authority over sickness and disease. The apostles continued this practice, using it to impart the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17), spiritual gifts (1 Timothy 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6), and blessings to believers. It also played a role in commissioning leaders and missionaries for ministry (Acts 13:3).
column5: In the New Testament, the laying on of hands is closely tied to the ministry of Jesus and the early church. Jesus regularly laid His hands on the sick to heal them (Mark 6:5, Luke 4:40), demonstrating compassion and power over sickness and disease. The apostles continued this practice, using it for the impartation of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17), spiritual gifts (1 Timothy 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6), and blessings directed to believers. It also played a role in appointing leaders and missionaries for the work of ministry (Acts 13:3).

column4: The laying on of hands symbolizes an act of faith and obedience to God’s Word. It is not a mechanical ritual, but a spiritual practice rooted in dependence on the Holy Spirit. For example, in Acts 6:6, the apostles laid hands on those selected to serve as deacons, committing them to God’s service and publicly acknowledging their calling. In Acts 19:6, Paul laid hands on believers, and they received the Holy Spirit, demonstrating its role in spiritual empowerment.

In Acts 19:6, Paul laid his hands on believers, and they received the Holy Spirit, showing his role in spiritual strengthening.

column4: ### Angels
column5: ### Angels

column4: Angels are a significant part of God’s creation, serving as His messengers and agents to carry out His divine purposes. The Bible reveals a spiritual realm inhabited by these beings, who are powerful, intelligent, and obedient to God’s commands. While angels are often unseen, their presence and actions impact human history and spiritual warfare. Understanding their roles, classifications, and activities provides us with deeper insight into God’s plan and the unseen realities that surround us.

Understanding their role, hierarchy, and functions gives us deep insight into God’s plan and the unseen realities that surround us.

column4: The term "angel" itself means "messenger," highlighting their primary function. Angels operate in obedience to God’s will, whether delivering messages, providing protection, executing judgment, or engaging in spiritual battles. They are not objects of worship but serve as examples of obedience and reverence, always pointing back to the glory of God. This chapter explores the nature, classifications, and roles of angels, shedding light on their significance in Scripture and in our lives today.

column4: In the scriptures angels are seen as **messengers**, **servants**, and **warriors**. Angels frequently act as messengers, delivering important announcements, warnings, and encouragements. They reveal God’s plans and provide guidance in times of need (Luke 1:26-38; Matthew 2:13; Revelation 1:1). Angels are actively involved in protecting, strengthening, and delivering believers. They minister to God’s people in times of distress and provide supernatural aid (Psalms 91:11; Acts 12:7-11; Matthew 4:11). Angels engage in spiritual warfare, battling demonic forces to advance God’s kingdom and defend believers (Daniel 10:13; Revelation 12:7-9).

column4: #### The Nature of Angels
column5: #### The Nature of Angels

column4: Angels are created beings, brought into existence by God before the foundation of the world. They are distinct from humans, possessing unique characteristics that equip them for their heavenly roles. The Bible teaches that angels are spiritual beings, not bound by physical limitations, yet they can take on visible forms when interacting with humans.

The Holy Bible teaches that angels are spiritual beings not bound by physical limitations, yet at times they can take on a visible form when interacting with people.

column4: Angels are described as immortal, meaning they do not die or age. They are innumerable, with vast hosts filling the heavenly realms. While they are often referred to with masculine pronouns, Scripture makes it clear that angels are sexless and do not marry or reproduce. These qualities emphasize their purpose as servants of God, entirely devoted to His will and commands. Angels possess remarkable traits that reflect their divine purpose. They are obedient, reverent, wise, and powerful. These qualities equip them to carry out God’s will effectively and faithfully.

column5: #### The Origin and Nature of Demons

column4: Demons are fallen angels who followed Satan’s rebellion against God. *(Revelation 12:7-9; Matthew 25:41).* Satan, formerly known as Lucifer (“light bearer”), an exalted angel, sought to exalt himself above God and was cast out of heaven along with other rebellious angels. *(Isaiah 14:12-15; Ezekiel 28:12-17).*

column4: Demons are spirits without physical bodies but can oppress and torment humans and animals. *(Mark 5:11-13).* They seek to deceive, tempt, oppress, and destroy. *(John 10:10; 2 Corinthians 11:14). column4: The gospels and epistles further clarify the work of the enemy. Evil spirits, as disembodied, largely must do their work through willing and open vessels. God works through people, so does the devil. This oppression is often marked by torment, self-harm, and destructive behaviors *(Luke 8:27-29).* Their attacks cause fear, temptation, and discouragement *(2 Corinthians 12:7).* The most common source of their power (not authority) in someone's life is through the influence of lies and emotional strongholds *(2 Corinthians 10:3-5).*

God works through people, and so does Satan. This oppression is often characterized by torment, self-harm, and destructive behaviors *(Luke 8:27-29).* Their attacks produce fear, temptation, and discouragement *(2 Corinthians 12:7).* The primary way their power (not authority) takes hold in a person’s life is through the influence of lies and emotional strongholds *(2 Corinthians 10:3-5).*

column4: It's important to note that not every lie a person believes, infirmity in their body, or stronghold in their life is the direct result of demonic influence, but these places of woundedness are places where the enemy can exploit us and keep us in a place of frustration and oppression.

column4: There are two major cautions in the scriptures when dealing with the demonic:
column5: There are two major warnings that Scripture gives when dealing with demons:

column4: 1. **Only those with a relationship with Jesus have the authority over the demonic**. Acts 19:11-20 talks about sons of a Jewish Chief Priest named Sceva. They tried to intervene in the life of someone who was oppressed and tormented by the devil and the evil spirit refused to leave because they didn’t have a relationship with Jesus. The man who was oppressed leapt on them, stripped them naked and beat them. Just as you should not impersonate a police officer, **don't impersonate someone with a relationship with Jesus, instead have a relationship with Jesus**!
column5: 1. **Only those who have a relationship with Jesus have authority over demons**. Acts 19:11-20 recounts the sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva. They tried to intervene in the life of a person whom the devil had oppressed and tormented, but the evil spirit refused to leave because they had no relationship with Jesus. The man who was oppressed leaped on them, stripped off their clothes, and beat them. Just as you wouldn’t pretend to be a police officer, **do not pretend to be someone who has a relationship with Jesus; instead, have a relationship with Jesus**!

column4: 2. **When an evil spirit leaves, it goes away for a time and will try to come back**. If it finds the place it had dwelled empty, it will come back worse. Matthew 12:43-45. When we minister to a person oppressed of the devil, that person needs to fill the void that evil spirit occupied in their lives. That means at a minimum establishing a personal relationship with Jesus and strengthening it by obedience to the Holy Spirit. Often an evil or unclean spirit has power to operate in someone’s life through the choices they made, based on their beliefs. Anyone delivered from the devil needs to replace that old belief system and be transformed by the renewal of their minds (Romans 12:1-2).
column5: 2. **When an evil spirit goes out, it leaves for a short time and tries to return**. If it finds the place it formerly inhabited empty, it will come back worse. Matthew 12:43-45. When we minister to someone oppressed by the devil, that person needs to fill the vacancy the evil spirit held in their life. At the very least, that means establishing a personal relationship with Jesus and strengthening obedience to the Holy Spirit. Many times an evil or unclean spirit gains power to operate in a person’s life through the choices they have made, based on their beliefs. Anyone delivered from the devil needs to replace their former belief system and be transformed by the renewing of their mind (Romans 12:1-2).

column4: We serve an awesome and mighty God, and we are ‘more than conquerors’ (Romans 8:37) over the defeated enemy. We have no need to fear our defeated enemy, for Jesus has given us His authority to crush his head! The devil’s time is short, and He will ultimately be judged along with every principality and power on the earth that rejects the dominion of Christ.
